newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's LDP, shy of majority, seeks ruling allies.
newsitem.headline: Japan's LDP, shy of majority, seeks ruling allies.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto began courting coalition partners on Monday after voters refused to give his Liberal Democratic Party a clear mandate in general elections.
Hashimoto's LDP on Sunday scored 239 seats, 12 short of the 251 it needed to govern alone in the 500-seat Lower House.

The LDP was expected to ask its two minority partners in the outgoing government, Sakigake and the Social Democrats, to stay in the ruling camp while sending feelers to the new Democratic Party, a group of young, reformist lawmakers.

The result dashed LDP hopes of regaining the grip on power it has enjoyed for most of the postwar period, and signalled more of the political turmoil that has plagued Japan since the 1993 election that put the LDP out of office.
In the end, Japan's 98 million voters decided to neither give the conservative LDP a mandate to govern alone nor gamble on throwing power to untested political parties.

"The result was that voters opted for a coalition centred on the LDP," said Kyodo news agency in an analysis. "In this transition period, voters sought political stability but did not want to restore the 1955 system of one-party LDP rule."
Their third choice was to stay away from the polls in record numbers, which led to a 59 percent voter turnout, the lowest figure since World War Two.
The election, held under a new system to clean up politics, had offered Japan the chance to end the lethargy caused by three years of unwieldy coalition wrangling.
But the hopes fizzled out into an inconclusive result likely to lead to more years of politics as usual and hamper efforts to reform the economy and bureaucracy.
"I think the LDP will be looking to run politics with few opponents, so policies will continue to take a long time to develop," said political analyst Minoru Morita.
The messy outcome leaves many unanswered questions about economic policies as the nation, emerging from a lengthy slump, struggles to clear a path to future growth.
The 28 seats the LDP added to the 211 it held in the old parliament ensured there would be no leadership challenge to Hashimoto, who has been prime minister since last January.

"We were not given a clear majority from voters, and we do not have a majority in the Upper House. Our stance is that we would welcome anybody or party (as coalition partners) that will agree with our policies," said a disappointed Hashimoto.
The horse trading, which could last for a week or more, started even before the final results were in.
"The LDP intends to begin (coalition) policy negotiations with Sakigake, the Social Democrats and also the Democrats," LDP secretary-general Koichi Kato said.
In the outgoing coalition government, the LDP was the dominant partner in a three-way alliance with the Social Democratic Party and Sakigake, a small LDP splinter group.
The LDP, which ruled Japan for 38 years until the last election in 1993, came back into government in mid-1994 in an unlikely alliance with the Socialists and Sakigake.

In order to command comfortable majorities in both houses of parliament, the LDP would need the Upper House seats held by the Social Democrats and the new Lower House seats won by the fledgling Democratic Party.

The two junior coalition partners won a total of 17 seats, less than half the number they held in the old parliament, while the one-month-old Democrats, formed by defectors from the two parties, claimed 52 seats.
The main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) dropped four seats to 156 and the future of the party and its leader Ichiro Ozawa, an LDP defector from 1993, was in doubt.
Shinshinto's main policy difference was to oppose an LDP plan to raise the sales tax to five percent from three percent next April. It also promised cuts in income taxes.

"It's not clear to me where major economic policies are now going," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia, citing such issues as tax reform, deregulation and provision for a rapidly ageing society.
The only clear winner in the poll was the Japan Communist Party, which nearly doubled its numbers to 26.

The election was held nearly one year ahead of schedule because of Hashimoto's belief that he could win sole power for the LDP amid an improving economy and success in cooling down opposition to the presence of U.S. troops in Okinawa.
A new electoral system, which replaced the old multi-seat constituencies, was also thought to favour the LDP at the expense of smaller parties.
Voters cast their ballots for 300 single-seat constituencies, while 200 seats were decided by proportional representation.
